study.title: 1 Chronicles 8 - The lineage of Benjamin and the house of Saul
study.overview: This chapter closes the genealogical series of 1 Chronicles with the tribe of Benjamin. The text brings together names, families and housing centers linked to this tribe, passing through ancient lineages, groups that inhabited near Jerusalem and Gibeon, and coming more in detail to Saul's family. The goal is not only to record ancestry, but to show how Benjamin remained linked to Israel's larger history, including the period of the monarchy, with emphasis on the continuity of its tribal inheritance.

outline.title: Initial descent of Benjamin
outline.explanation: The first verses list the children of Benjamin and the descendants of Bela. The repetition of names and the short structure show the genealogical function of the text: preserve lineages within the tribe and record family continuity.

outline.title: Clans, displacements and housing cores
outline.explanation: Here are families of Ehud and Saharaim, with references to Moab, Geba, Ono, Lode and Aijalom. The text associates genealogy to places and also to military or expulsion actions, indicating that these families are not only names, but groups with concrete presence in specific regions.

outline.title: Heads of families in Jerusalem and Gibeon
outline.explanation: The list continues with various descendants of Shimei, Shasac, and Jeroam, concludes the heads of families who lived in Jerusalem and then describes the house of Gibeon and its inhabitants neighboring Jerusalem. The contrast between the two centers shows the distribution of the tribe in the region.

outline.title: The genealogy of Saul and the sons of Ulam
outline.explanation: The final part leads Saul through Kish and Ner, then follows the descendants of Saul to Meribe-Baal and Micah, arriving at the sons of Ulam. The closure highlights that these descendants were brave warriors and had many descendants, reaffirming the permanence of the Benjamite lineage.

study.context: According to the notes, this chapter concludes the genealogical record begun earlier with Judah and closes it with Benjamin, the tribe of Saul. There is also the observation that Benjamin was connected to Jerusalem and, in part, to the period of exile and return. The notes do not allow to safely determine more historical details, but make it clear that the chronicler preserves traditions of tribal families, places and memories to show continuity between Israel's ancient history and later life.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter values God's faithfulness in preserving a people through concrete genealogies. Even when the text seems only a sequence of names, it states that the history of Israel is neither chaotic nor forgotten: there is continuity between generations, between territory and people, and between tribal past and monarchy. The inclusion of Saul's house, although Saul was the first king before the dynasty of David, shows that the biblical memory does not erase the historical dignity of his lineage. At the same time, the focus is not on exalting individuals, but to place them within God's greater purpose for his people. The mention of brave warriors and numerous families also suggests that strength, fertility and permanence are seen as providential gifts, not as autonomous merits.

scholarViews.insight: The record ends with Benjamin to shut down the genealogies, for the book began with Judah, the tribe of David, and now concludes with Benjamin, the tribe of Saul.
The chapter highlights Saul's family because the first king of Israel comes from him, and because the tribe of Benjamin played a relevant role in Jerusalem and the return of captivity.
The comment suggests that the passage about the sons of Ulão presents them as brave men, and notes that the text underlines the honor and numerous descent of that family.

questions: What does the detailing of names and families teach about the importance of community memory in the biblical faith?
Why does the chronicler close the genealogies with Benjamin and give special attention to Saul's house?
How does the presence of Benjaminite families in Jerusalem help to understand the continuity of God's people?
study.practice: Read your own story in the light of God's faithfulness to generations. Pray for your family, forgotten names and people in your community who support the work in a discreet way. If possible, record the story of your faith and your home, remembering that the Lord works through real bonds, not just major events. It is also worth cultivating gratitude for the spiritual inheritance received and responsibility to convey it with integrity.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is predominantly genealogical, and several exact relationships between some names and lineages remain obscure in the text itself. The notes provided also indicate uncertainties in some names and possible textual variants, especially in parallel passages. Therefore, some identifications remain as a probable reading, not as absolute certainty.
